title: Cutting the Pages

post.author: u/hobcarr_mill_henrike
post.title: I repair old books by candlelight in a converted mill. Our assistant told my apprentice an arsenic binding was fine to handle, in my own words, from a page that says the opposite.

blocks.text: I'm a book conservator. My studio is the top floor of Hobcarr Mill, and I work late, because the best light for reading a damaged cover is raking light, one candle held low, so every scuff throws a shadow. Last winter I typed up the binder's manual we have worked from since it was printed in 1863, with my studio notes after the chapters they belong to, so my two apprentices could ask an assistant instead of waiting for me.

I built it the way the séance thread on this board described. My script cut the handbook into pieces of 500 characters each, roughly 125 tokens, end to end, and embedded every piece. Each piece keeps its source as metadata: the manual, 1863, or my notes, 2025. A question pulls the three closest pieces, and a model answers from them.

On Tuesday Kezia was laying out a ledger in for repair: a corn merchant's account book of 1858, bound in bright green cloth. She held it against the colour swatch bookmark from the Poison Book Project that hangs by the bench. It matched the emerald. At 21:52 she typed:

21:52  kezia      Is the emerald green cloth on the 1858 ledger safe to handle?
21:52  assistant  Yes. Handle it freely, and wash your hands after, as for any old book.

She had it open on the bench, bare-handed, when I came up the stairs with the candle. I wrote page 42 myself: bindings of this colour from the 1840s to the 1860s may carry arsenic, and you handle them only with nitrile gloves. She washed, and I sealed the ledger in a bag.
It answered in my sentences, and every one of them was in the book. Just not together.

The words it used are on page 43, under Other green cloths, about cloth made after 1900. On Wednesday night I printed the pieces my script had made from pages 40 to 47, numbered from 1, and looked at where the cuts fell.

diagram.aria: Henrike's printout of three pieces from pages 40 to 47. Piece 2, ranked second and sent, ends with the heading Emerald green cloths. A cut at character 1,000. Piece 3, ranked fifth of six and not sent, holds the warning from page 42, gloves only, with no heading and no word green. A cut at character 1,500. Piece 4, ranked first and sent, holds Other green cloths from page 43: handle it freely. Below piece 4, the reply at 21:52: yes, handle it freely, answered from rank 1.

blocks.caption: Printed on Wednesday night. Pages 40 to 47 made six pieces. Piece 2 ends with the heading Emerald green cloths; the cut falls right after it, at character 1,000. Piece 3 is the whole warning from page 42 and never says green. For Kezia's question the three pieces sent were piece 4 (Other green cloths, page 43), piece 2, and piece 5 (lifting cloth from the boards). Piece 3 came fifth of six.

blocks.text: Four hundred more books from the studio's library are waiting to go in. How should I cut the pages?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Glad she's all right. What your script does has a name: chunking, splitting a document into pieces, called chunks, that are embedded and searched one at a time. The search never sees the page, only the chunk. Your chunk size is 500 characters, and you have no overlap: overlap is when each chunk repeats a little of the end of the one before. Two questions. What is the last line of piece 2, and the first line of piece 3? And when the model answered from piece 4, what did it know about where that text sat in the handbook?

replies.author: u/hobcarr_mill_henrike
replies.text: Piece 2 ends with the heading, Emerald green cloths, and then the cut. Piece 3 starts: Bindings of this colour made from the 1840s to the 1860s may be coloured with copper acetoarsenite. Then: Handle it only with nitrile gloves, never bare-handed. Which colour, it doesn't say. As for where: each piece knew its source and year, my notes, 2025, and nothing else. Not the heading, not the page.

comments.author: u/just_use_512_bettany
comments.text: You're overthinking it. 512 tokens with 50 overlap is the standard; half the tutorials and libraries ship with it. Your 500 characters is tiny, that's the whole bug. Use the default and the heading and the warning land in the same chunk. Hand-tuning a splitter for every book is how you never finish 400 books.

replies.author: u/hobcarr_mill_henrike
replies.text: Wouldn't a 512-token piece hold half a dozen sections at once?

replies.author: u/just_use_512_bettany
replies.text: Sure, and the model reads them all. That's what the context window is for.

comments.author: u/kezia_at_the_bench
comments.text: I'm the apprentice. I asked because the cloth matched the swatch exactly and I wanted to be sure. The answer sounded like Henrike: the same words she uses, wash your hands after. That's why I believed it.

replies.author: u/hobcarr_mill_henrike
replies.text: It was my sentence. Just not about your book.

reply.prompt: Four hundred more books are waiting. How should Henrike cut the pages before they go in? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Make each chapter one chunk, so a warning is never parted from its heading and the model reads it all.
options.part2: Henrike cut the handbook by chapter: pages 40 to 47 became three chunks, and with three sent for every question, all of it went every time. Kezia's question came back right this time, from the Pigments and safety chapter. Then she wrote six test questions with known right sections. Asked which paste to use on cloth, the assistant answered: for an account book in daily use, choose buckram. The thread question got the same answer. Covering materials mentions cloth again and again, and threads once, so it outranked the Repairs chapter, where paste and thread share the pages with mending, lifting and storage. Each question now carried 1,005 input tokens in the sample instead of 695, and the real chapters run to dozens of pages.
options.senior: A chunk is embedded as one vector, so a chapter about six things matches each of them weakly, and the chapter that mentions a word most often wins. Big chunks also fill every prompt with text the question doesn't need, which costs tokens and buries the answer in the middle. Nothing is cut, and nothing is sharp.

options.text: Make each sentence one chunk, so that every match is precise and nothing else waters down the warning's score.
options.part2: Henrike cut one sentence per chunk: pages 40 to 47 became 38. Kezia asked again. The best match was the line Emerald green cloths itself, a heading with nothing under it. Second came a sentence about later green cloth, third the heading Other green cloths. The warning, Handle it only with nitrile gloves, never bare-handed, matched nothing: on its own it doesn't say which cloth it is about. The assistant said it couldn't find a rule for that. Five of her six test questions passed, which looked fine, until she saw that the one that failed was Kezia's.
options.senior: Small chunks lose the context that makes them mean something: a sentence that says it or this no longer says what it refers to, and a heading alone matches well and says nothing. Precision in the score is not precision in the answer. The fix is to give small pieces their context, not to make them smaller.

options.text: Cut every book by hand, reading each page yourself, so no warning is ever parted from its own heading.
options.verdict: Right, and a year of evenings
options.part2: Henrike cut the handbook by hand over three evenings, a section per chunk, with the section's headings and page written at the top of each. Kezia's question came back with the warning, and all six test questions passed. Then she opened the first box of the library. At one book an evening, 400 books is more than a year of evenings, and every corrected edition means cutting it again. By the second week she was cutting faster, and less carefully.
options.senior: Her hand cuts were right because she cut where the author cut: at the headings and paragraphs. That rule can be written down and run by a splitter, and then checked with test questions. Spend the human time on the test set and on the odd book with no structure, not on every page.

options.text: Split on headings, then paragraphs; keep heading and page on each chunk; overlap a sentence; test it.
options.part2: Henrike set her splitter to cut at the handbook's headings first, then at paragraphs, up to 125 tokens a chunk, with one sentence of overlap, and every chunk carrying its section path and page. Kezia's question came back: Handle it only with nitrile gloves, never bare-handed. Source: Pigments and safety > Emerald green cloths, p. 42. She wrote six questions whose right sections she knew: 6 of 6 retrieved, 6 of 6 answered from the right rule, at 563 input tokens a question, fewer than before. The overlap sends 14 tokens twice. Now every book runs the test set before it goes in, with a question for every warning in it.
options.senior: Cut where the author cut, so each chunk holds one idea with its own context; carry the heading and page so the search and the reader both know where a chunk sits; add a little overlap where a cut must fall inside a section; and measure the split with known questions, because scores look fine right up to the question that matters.

sim.title: Cut the Hobcarr handbook yourself
sim.lede: You're Henrike on Wednesday night, with pages 40 to 47 of the handbook: 3 chapters, 9 sections, 11 paragraphs, 2,743 characters. There is no real model and no real embedding. A stand-in embedding counts 9 keywords in each chunk (emerald, green, cloth, arsenic, box, lift, paste, thread, account), and a chunk's score is the cosine similarity of its counts and the question's, so every score is exact. This exaggerates the loss: a chunk with none of the question's keywords scores 0.00, where a real embedding would still give it a partial match. The rest of the handbook scores lower for every question here, a teaching simplification. The top 3 chunks are sent, and a stand-in answers from the first of them that holds a whole rule. Pick a splitter: fixed characters, which cuts every so many characters wherever that falls; recursive, which tries to cut at a heading, then a paragraph, then a sentence, then a space, and fills each chunk up to the size; by heading, a section per chunk; a whole chapter each; or one sentence each. Set the chunk size in tokens (a teaching value of 4 characters a token), the overlap, and whether each chunk keeps its heading and page. The test set is six questions whose right rules are known. Tokens per question: a 300-token system prompt, a 20-token question, and the chunks sent.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on Tuesday's cuts: fixed characters, 125 tokens (500 characters), no overlap, no heading. Kezia's question sends chunks 4, 2 and 5 at 0.84, 0.79 and 0.56; chunk 3, the warning, scores 0.00 and comes fifth. The answer: handle it freely. Test set: 4 of 6 retrieved, 3 of 6 right, 695 tokens. Keep heading and page: chunk 3 scores 0.87 and wins, 5 of 6 and 5 of 6. Turn that off and set overlap to 25 tokens instead: the heading rides across the cut, 6 of 6 and 5 of 6. Try a whole chapter each: 6 of 6 retrieved, 4 of 6 right, 1,005 tokens. One sentence each: the heading alone scores 1.00, the warning 0.00, nothing found. Fixed, 512 tokens, overlap 50: two chunks, 4 of 6 right, and Kezia's question answered from Calico and buckram. Then by heading, 125 tokens, overlap 25, heading and page kept: 6 of 6 and 6 of 6, at 563 tokens.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the handbook changed. A cut every 500 characters fell just after the heading Emerald green cloths, so the warning sat alone in a chunk that never said green, ranked fifth and was never sent, and the closest green chunk was the one about cloth made after 1900.

steps.title: The search sees chunks, never pages.
steps.text: Chunking splits a document into chunks that are embedded and searched one at a time, so each chunk has to make sense on its own. Henrike's warning did on the page, under its heading. Cut away from it, piece 3 said: bindings of this colour may carry arsenic; handle it only with nitrile gloves. Which colour? Nothing in the chunk says. Kezia's question was about emerald green cloth, and the chunk that answered it best, by its words, was Other green cloths. Piece 5, sent third, did say never lift an emerald green cloth outside a fume hood, but that is about lifting, and the model answered from the top piece.

steps.title: Chunk size is a trade, counted in tokens.
steps.text: Size chunks in tokens, the unit embedding models and prompts are limited and billed in. Too small, and a chunk loses its context: Handle it only with nitrile gloves no longer says what it is. Too big, and one vector has to stand for several topics, so it matches each of them weakly; and every chunk sent fills the prompt, which costs tokens and pushes the useful lines into the middle, where case 4 of Season 2 and Liu and colleagues' lost in the middle finding say models use them less well. In the lab, a whole chapter each sends 1,005 tokens for Kezia's question and still answers two of six from the wrong chapter. There is no single right number: the thread's 512 is one figure you will see, OpenAI's vector stores default to 800, and the right size depends on how long one idea runs in your documents.

steps.title: Overlap patches a cut, and costs.
steps.text: Overlap repeats a sentence or two from the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so a thought cut in two still appears whole somewhere. In the lab, 25 tokens of overlap on Tuesday's fixed-size chunking carries the heading Emerald green cloths into the warning's chunk, and Kezia's question comes back right; that was luck of where the cut fell, not design. The cost is more chunks to embed and store, and near-duplicate results: two chunks that share their edges can take two of the three places sent, and the same text is paid for twice.

steps.title: Cut where the author cut, and keep where it came from.
steps.text: Structure-aware splitting cuts at the document's own seams: headings first, then paragraphs, then sentences, and only then words. A recursive splitter does this with a list of separators tried in order; LangChain's default list is a blank line, a line break, a space, then single characters, and a list that starts with headings suits a handbook. Then carry the structure as metadata, the way the séance case kept writer and date: each chunk keeps its section path and page, sits in front of the chunk's text when it is embedded, and is shown under the answer. With that, Kezia's question finds the warning at Pigments and safety > Emerald green cloths, p. 42.

steps.title: Test the split, not only the answers.
steps.text: Run a retrieval test set, questions whose right sections you know, against every chunking choice: fixed or structural, the size, the overlap, the heading on or off. Henrike's six questions show Tuesday's cuts at 4 of 6 retrieved and 3 of 6 right, and the new split at 6 of 6 and 6 of 6, at fewer tokens. Two ideas build on this later. Contextual retrieval, case 7 of this season, adds a short summary of the document to each chunk before embedding. Parent-child retrieval, also called small-to-big retrieval, searches small chunks and sends the larger section each one sits in.

diagram.aria: The fix. Page 42 of the handbook, a heading and two paragraphs, goes into a splitter that cuts at headings, then paragraphs, then sentences. It makes chunk 4, 80 tokens, the heading and the warning, and chunk 5, 95 tokens, which starts with the warning carried over by one sentence of overlap; both carry Pigments and safety > Emerald green cloths, p. 42. Kezia's question scores chunk 5 at 1.00 and chunk 4 at 0.96. The answer: nitrile gloves only, with its source, page 42. A test set of six known questions checks the splitter: 6 of 6 right.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn from the lab's senior settings. Page 42 is cut at its own heading and paragraph break. Chunk 4 holds the heading with the warning; chunk 5 holds the second paragraph and starts with the warning again, carried over by one sentence of overlap. Both carry their section path and page. Kezia's question scores them 1.00 and 0.96, and the answer shows page 42. The test set checks the splitter, not just the answers.

fix.title: The fix: cut at the book's own seams, carry the heading and page, and test the cut
fix.text: Split each book at its headings, then its paragraphs, then sentences only where a paragraph is too long, up to a size measured in tokens (125 suits the handbook's short sections). Never merge across a heading. Repeat one sentence across a cut inside a section. Give every chunk its section path and page as metadata, put the path in front of the text when you embed it, and show it under the answer, so Kezia can see page 42 and Henrike can see when a source looks wrong. Before any book goes in, run a test set of questions with known right sections, with at least one question for every warning in the book, and run it again after any change to the splitter, the size or the overlap.

limits: The lab exaggerates the loss. Its keyword counts give piece 3 a score of 0.00 because it never says emerald, green or cloth; a real embedding would still give it a partial match from arsenic, pigment and gloves, and might have ranked it fourth instead of fifth. On Tuesday it still wasn't in the top three, and a partial match is not a reliable one.

Structure only helps where there is structure. A scanned book whose extracted text lost its headings, a table split across pages, or a letter-book with no headings at all needs its structure recovered, or written in by hand, before a structural splitter has seams to cut at.

Every chunk in a section now carries the same heading, so a chunk with little but the heading can outrank the one that holds the rule: in the lab, the second paragraph of the emerald section scores 1.00 and the warning's own chunk 0.96. The overlap is what puts the warning in both; the test set is what tells you it worked.

Needs documents with structure, and a test set someone has to write and keep up.

explain.seniorTake: A chunk is the only thing the search ever sees, so it has to carry its own meaning: one idea, cut at the author's seams, with the heading and page that say where it sits. Size it in tokens for how long an idea runs in your documents, not for a number from a tutorial; add a little overlap where a cut has to fall mid-section; and judge every choice with a test set of known questions, because a split can look fine on average and still lose the one sentence that matters.

realWorld.title: The Poison Book Project: emerald green bookcloth
realWorld.text: The Poison Book Project, run by Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library and the University of Delaware, says that in early 2019 analysis of 19th-century, cloth-case publishers' bindings at Winterthur Library revealed bookcloth colored with emerald green, or copper acetoarsenite, an inorganic pigment known to be extremely toxic. Its list of trends for such bookcloth gives publication dates primarily between 1840s-1860s, which is why the ledger in the story is dated 1858.

realWorld.title: The Poison Book Project: handling
realWorld.text: Its handling tips say to wear nitrile gloves and to avoid handling suspected arsenical green books with bare hands, and that even when gloves have been used, to wash hands thoroughly with soap and water afterwards. For conservators it warns that mechanical manipulation such as lifting the cloth from its board support can result in spalling of arsenical pigment dust, and advises working under a certified chemical fume hood. Henrike's pages 42 and 45 follow this advice.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: the default chunk size and overlap
realWorld.text: OpenAI's retrieval guide says that by default, max_chunk_size_tokens is set to 800 and chunk_overlap_tokens is set to 400, meaning every file is indexed by being split up into 800-token chunks, with 400-token overlap between consecutive chunks. You can change it with chunking_strategy; max_chunk_size_tokens must be between 100 and 4096 inclusive, and chunk_overlap_tokens should not exceed max_chunk_size_tokens / 2. So there is no single standard: OpenAI's own default is 800 with 400, not 512 with 50.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a chunk that lost its context
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Introducing Contextual Retrieval post (September 2024) says traditional RAG solutions remove context when encoding information, which often results in the system failing to retrieve the relevant information from the knowledge base. Its example chunk is: The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter. On its own, the post says, it doesn't specify which company it's referring to or the relevant time period. It also says the choice of chunk size, chunk boundary, and chunk overlap can affect retrieval performance. The method it proposes belongs to case 7 of this season.

realWorld.title: LangChain: the recursive splitter's separators
realWorld.text: LangChain's documentation calls its recursive character text splitter the recommended one for generic text. It is parameterized by a list of characters and tries to split on them in order until the chunks are small enough; the default list is a blank line, a line break, a space and an empty string. This has the effect of trying to keep all paragraphs (and then sentences, and then words) together as long as possible. On overlap it says overlapping chunks helps to mitigate loss of information when context is divided between chunks.

realWorld.title: LangChain: splitting on headings, keeping them as metadata
realWorld.text: LangChain's guide to splitting markdown says chunking often aims to keep text with common context together, so we might want to specifically honor the structure of the document itself. Its header splitter will split a markdown file by a specified set of headers, and header information is retained in the metadata for each document, the same idea as Henrike's section path.

realWorld.title: Lost in the middle, again
realWorld.text: Liu and colleagues found in 2023 that performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and degrades when it is in the middle (case 9 of Season 1). Chunks that are too big pad every prompt with text the question doesn't need, and the line that answers it can land in that middle.

asked: How do you choose a chunk size?
What goes wrong when chunks are too small or too big?
How would you chunk a long PDF manual with headings and tables?
interview.answer: I'd start from the documents, not a number. Look at how long one idea runs: a handbook's sections might be a hundred tokens, a legal contract's clauses much longer. Size in tokens, because that's what embedding models and prompts are limited and billed in. Too small and a chunk loses its context: a sentence like handle it only with gloves no longer says what it is about, and a heading alone can match best while saying nothing. Too big and one vector stands for several topics, so it matches each weakly, and every chunk sent pads the prompt, which costs tokens and buries the answer in the middle. For a long PDF manual I'd first recover the structure: headings from the PDF's outline or font sizes, and tables kept as tables. Then split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences only where a paragraph is too long, never across a heading, with a sentence of overlap inside a section. Keep each table whole if it fits; otherwise split it by rows and repeat the header row in every piece. Every chunk carries its section path and page as metadata, embedded with the text and shown with the answer. Then I'd build a test set of questions with known right sections, including questions about exceptions and table cells, and compare a few sizes and overlaps on it. Defaults differ: OpenAI's file search uses 800 tokens with 400 overlap, and tutorials often show smaller figures such as 512 with 50. I'd pick whichever scores best on my own questions, and rerun the test whenever the documents or the splitter change.

terms.def: A person trained to repair and preserve old books and papers so they last, changing as little of the original as possible. Henrike is one.
A building where grain was once ground or cloth once made, often by a river. Hobcarr Mill's top floor is now Henrike's studio.
Someone learning a craft by working beside a skilled person. Kezia is one of Henrike's two.
A printed book of instructions for bookbinders. Henrike's was printed in 1863; her studio has worked from it ever since.
Here, Henrike's typed-up binder's manual with her studio notes added after the chapters they belong to. The assistant answers from it.
Henrike's own written rules for her studio, such as the emerald green pages, typed into the handbook in 2025.
Cloth made for covering books, usually stiffened and often embossed with a grain. Publishers used it widely from the 19th century on.
A bright green pigment of the 19th century, copper acetoarsenite, which contains arsenic. It was used in bookcloth, wallpaper and clothing.
The chemical name of emerald green: a copper and arsenic compound. On bookcloth it rubs off easily as a fine dust.
A poisonous element. Swallowed, breathed in, or over time through the skin, it can make people ill.
Thin disposable gloves made of a synthetic rubber. The Poison Book Project advises them for handling suspected arsenical books.
A ventilated cabinet that draws dust and fumes away from the person working in it.
A bookmark printed with known shades of a colour. The Poison Book Project hands them out so people can compare a green binding with emerald green.
A research project of Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library and the University of Delaware that finds and studies 19th-century books with toxic colorants.
Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library in Delaware, United States, a museum with a large library of historic books.
A trader who bought and sold grain. His ledger, an account book of 1858, is the book on Kezia's bench.
A plain, cheap cotton cloth. The handbook uses it for the inner joints of a binding.
Cotton or linen cloth stiffened with size so it wears well. The handbook advises it for account books in daily use.
Splitting a document into pieces, called chunks, that are embedded, stored and searched one at a time in a RAG system.
One piece made by chunking. The search compares the question with each chunk on its own, so a chunk must make sense on its own. Henrike says piece.
The most a chunk may hold, best counted in tokens. Henrike's was 500 characters, roughly 125 tokens.
Text repeated at the start of a chunk from the end of the one before, so a thought cut in two still appears whole in one chunk.
Here, the place where one chunk ends and the next begins. Henrike's script cut at every 500th character, wherever that fell.
Cutting a document every so many characters or tokens, with no regard for sentences, paragraphs or headings.
The code that does the chunking: it decides where each cut falls.
What a splitter may cut at, such as a heading, a blank line between paragraphs, the end of a sentence, or a space.
A splitter that tries its separators in order, cutting at the first that makes pieces small enough: headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, then words.
Chunking that cuts at a document's own seams, such as headings, sections and paragraphs, instead of at a character count.
The chain of headings above a piece of text, such as Pigments and safety > Emerald green cloths. Kept as metadata with each chunk.
A result that is almost the same as another, such as two chunks that share their overlapping sentences.
The lab's script in place of an embedding model: it counts 9 stated keywords in each chunk. It is a teaching simplification and measures nothing.
How many times each of a fixed list of words appears in a text. The lab's stand-in embedding is a keyword count; a word counts when it starts with the keyword.
OpenAI's setting for how files in a vector store are cut: the chunk size and overlap, in tokens.
OpenAI's name for the chunk size in a vector store's chunking strategy. Default 800; allowed 100 to 4096.
OpenAI's name for the overlap between consecutive chunks. Default 400; no more than half the chunk size.
An open-source library for building applications on language models. It includes several text splitters.
A plain-text format where lines starting with # mark headings. Splitters can use those marks to find a document's sections.
Anthropic's 2024 method of adding a short, document-aware summary to each chunk before embedding it. Case 7 of this season covers it.
Searching small chunks for sharp matches, then sending the larger section each one belongs to. Also called small-to-big retrieval.
Another name for parent-child retrieval.
The book of instructions that comes with a product, often long, with sections, tables and exceptions.
The part of a rule that names when it doesn't apply: fits every pump, except those made before 2019.
The first row of a table, naming what each column holds.
A cloth maker's book of numbered samples, with a table of each pattern's details.
Light shone low across a surface, so every bump and scuff throws a shadow. Henrike uses one candle held low.
Here, a pattern pressed into bookcloth, such as a morocco grain made to look like goatskin.
A thin glue or starch brushed into cloth or paper to stiffen it. Not the same as chunk size: the handbook's buckram is stiffened with size.
The stiff panels, often of card, that form a book's front and back covers under the cloth.
Strips of linen that a book's sections are sewn onto, so it opens flat and the cover can hold it.
Thin, strong paper with long fibres, used by conservators to mend tears almost invisibly.
A smooth, flat tool, once made of bone, for creasing paper and rubbing down cloth and paper.
A cabinet of wide, shallow drawers for keeping large flat sheets, such as cloth offcuts.
A leftover piece cut from a larger sheet of cloth or paper, kept for patching.
Paper or cloth glued along the back of a book's sewn pages to strengthen the spine.
An adhesive cooked from wheat starch and water. Conservators like it because water can undo it later.
A coloured powder mixed into a material to colour it. Emerald green is one.
Flaking or chipping off in small pieces. Lifting emerald green cloth can spall arsenical dust.
A cover put on many copies of a book at once by the publisher, usually boards covered in bookcloth, also called a cloth-case binding.
The clause of the quality standard on controlling documented information, including that it is available and suitable for use where and when it is needed.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that answers from long documents: a support bot over a product manual, an internal handbook search, an on-call helper over runbooks. A common incident: a support bot tells a customer that a part fits their model, because the manual's except clause, not for models made before 2019, sat at the top of the next chunk, and the chunk that was sent read as a plain yes. Look at how your documents are cut. Is it a fixed count of characters or tokens, or the documents' own headings and paragraphs? Does each chunk know its section and page, and is that shown under the answer? Is there a test set of questions with known right sections, including exceptions and table cells, run whenever the splitter or the documents change? Fix it by splitting by section, keeping the heading and page with every chunk, and adding a known-answer test for every exception before it goes live. Standards-readiness note: if your company holds or is pursuing ISO 9001:2015 certification, clause 7.5.3 asks that documented information be available and suitable for use where and when it is needed; an assistant that presents half a rule as the whole rule is the kind of gap an auditor raises, so keep each answer's section and page traceable from the first build rather than at audit time. In the crossover season, Nightwatch's Build Night X1 builds an incident copilot with RAG over runbooks, and it splits each runbook by heading, so every chunk keeps the alarm and step it belongs to.

recall.prompt: Your support bot answers customers from a 300-page product manual, cut into pieces of 1,000 characters end to end. A customer asked whether the X20 filter fits their Model 4 pump, and the bot said yes. The manual says the X20 fits every Model 4 pump, except those made before 2019, and the customer's pump is from 2017. The words except those made before 2019 open the next piece. What went wrong, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The cut fell inside the rule, so the piece that was sent held the rule without its exception
Split along the manual's structure, by section and paragraph, so a rule and its exceptions stay in one chunk
Keep the section heading and page with every chunk and show them with the answer
Test with known questions, including exceptions, whenever the split changes

recall.model: The cut fell inside the rule. Pieces of 1,000 characters are cut wherever the count lands, so the sentence about the X20 ended in one piece and its exception opened the next. The bot was sent the piece that read as a plain yes. I'd change the splitter to work by section: cut at the manual's headings, then paragraphs, and only then sentences, so a rule and its exceptions stay together in one chunk, with a sentence of overlap where a long section has to be cut. Every chunk keeps its section path and page as metadata, embedded with the text and shown under the answer, so the customer and our staff can see which section a yes came from. Then I'd build a test set of known questions with known right sections, including one for every exception in the manual, like the pre-2019 pumps, and run it every time the split or the manual changes.

recall.prompt: Why did the assistant tell Kezia the emerald green cloth was fine to handle?
options: The model read the warning and chose to ignore it.
The warning sat in a chunk with no heading and no word green, so it ranked fifth and was never sent.
The embedding model has never seen the word emerald.
Page 43 of the handbook is wrong about green cloth.
recall.why: The cut every 500 characters fell just after the heading Emerald green cloths. The warning's chunk said only bindings of this colour and handle it only with nitrile gloves, so it matched Kezia's question poorly, came fifth of six and was not among the three sent. The top chunk was Other green cloths, about cloth made after 1900, and the model answered from it.

recall.prompt: A teammate is setting up retrieval over the company wiki and asks you: how do you choose a chunk size, and what goes wrong when chunks are too small or too big?

keyIdeas.idea: Too small and a chunk loses its context: a sentence no longer says what it refers to
Too big and one vector stands for several topics, matching each weakly, and every chunk sent costs tokens and buries the answer
There is no universal number: start from how long an idea runs in the documents, count in tokens, and compare sizes on a test set

recall.model: I'd start from the wiki, not from a number. Look at how long one idea usually runs, a page section or a few paragraphs, and size chunks in tokens, since that's what embedding models and prompts are limited and billed in. Too small and a chunk loses its context: a sentence like turn it off first no longer says what it refers to, and a heading on its own can match best while saying nothing. Too big and one vector stands for several topics, so it matches each of them weakly, and every chunk sent costs more tokens and can leave the line that answers the question lost in the middle of a long prompt. Defaults differ, 800 tokens in OpenAI's vector stores and smaller figures such as 512 in tutorials, so I'd try a few sizes, split on the wiki's headings and paragraphs, and compare them on a test set of known questions with known right pages.

recall.prompt: Henrike adds a sentence of overlap between chunks. What does it cost?
options: More chunks, the same text embedded and sent twice, and near-duplicates that can crowd the top results.
Every chunk's embedding becomes less accurate.
The section titles are dropped from the chunks.
recall.why: Overlap repeats the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so a cut thought still appears whole somewhere. The bill is more chunks to embed and store, the repeated text paid for again in every prompt that sends both, and near-duplicate results taking places in the top k. In the lab's senior settings the overlap sends 14 tokens twice for Kezia's question.

recall.prompt: Kezia's question is answered right at last. What tells Henrike the new split will keep working as the 400 books go in?
options: The top score for Kezia's question is now 1.00.
Running a test set of questions with known right sections, including one for every warning, before each book goes in and after any change to the splitter.
Reading every chunk of every book herself.
Using a larger chunk size so that nothing is cut.
recall.why: A high score for one question says nothing about the others, and in the lab a chunk with little but its heading can score 1.00. A retrieval test set checks the split itself: did the chunk holding the right rule come back in the top k, and did the answer come from it? Run it per book and after every change to the splitter, the size or the overlap.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. 212 of the 400 books are in, cut at their headings and paragraphs, each chunk carrying its section and page, and all 40 check questions pass. Last week we added a cloth maker's pattern book from the 1850s: one long table of 80 numbered patterns, with columns for colour, first year, last year, and arsenic found. Its only heading is at the top. Rufus asked whether pattern 47 was safe to handle. The assistant answered: Yes. The source shown was the pattern book, page 9. I printed the chunk. It begins at pattern 41 and holds rows like 47 | dark green | 1854 | 1861 | yes. The table's top line, the one that says what each column means, is in the first chunk, on page 8, not in this one.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the assistant say yes about pattern 47, and how should tables like this be chunked?

keyIdeas.idea: The table was cut into runs of rows without the header row, so the yes lost its column name and read as an answer
Keep a table whole if it fits, otherwise split by rows and repeat the header row and the table's title in every piece
Treat a table as structure of its own: write each row out with its column names so every value says what it is
Add table questions to the test set, including ones whose answer sits in a later row

coldCase.model: The yes was arsenic found, not safe. The splitter treated the table as one long paragraph and cut it into runs of rows, and only the first run kept the header row, so the chunk with pattern 47 held values with no column names, and the model read the last one as an answer to Rufus. Tables need cutting by their own structure. Keep a table whole if it fits in a chunk; if it doesn't, split it by rows and repeat the header row, and the table's title, in every piece. Better still for retrieval, write each row out with its column names, so pattern 47 reads as colour dark green, first year 1854, last year 1861, arsenic found yes. Keep the section and page on every piece as now. Then add table questions to the test set, including ones whose answer sits deep in the table, and run it before the next pattern book goes in. Pattern 47 goes in a sealed bag, handled with nitrile gloves.

sources.title: The Poison Book Project (Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library and the University of Delaware), Arsenical bookbindings, read 11 October 2026: in early 2019, analysis of 19th-century, cloth-case publishers' bindings at Winterthur Library revealed bookcloth colored with emerald green, or copper acetoarsenite, an inorganic pigment known to be extremely toxic; publication dates primarily between 1840s-1860s; emerald green publishers' bindings present a health risk and should be identified, handled, and stored with caution

The Poison Book Project, Handling and safety tips, read 11 October 2026: wear nitrile gloves; avoid handling suspected arsenical green books with bare hands; even when gloves have been used, wash hands thoroughly with soap and water; seal the book in a zip-top, polyethylene baggie; mechanical manipulation such as lifting the cloth from its board support can result in spalling of arsenical pigment dust; work under a certified chemical fume hood

OpenAI, Retrieval guide (developer docs), read 11 October 2026: by default, max_chunk_size_tokens is set to 800 and chunk_overlap_tokens is set to 400; you can adjust this by setting chunking_strategy; max_chunk_size_tokens must be between 100 and 4096 inclusive; chunk_overlap_tokens must be non-negative and should not exceed max_chunk_size_tokens / 2

Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval, Anthropic Engineering, published 19 September 2024, read 11 October 2026: traditional RAG solutions remove context when encoding information; example chunk, The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter; the choice of chunk size, chunk boundary, and chunk overlap can affect retrieval performance

LangChain documentation, Splitting recursively (text splitter integration guide), read 11 October 2026: the recommended splitter for generic text; parameterized by a list of characters, tried in order until the chunks are small enough; default list a blank line, a line break, a space, an empty string; overlapping chunks helps to mitigate loss of information

LangChain documentation, Split markdown (text splitter integration), read 11 October 2026: chunking often aims to keep text with common context together; honor the structure of the document itself; header information is retained in the metadata for each document
